assessment.rationale: For this lower-layer geofencing case, the variant is a good envelope-level fit: Bob can retain and forward encrypted condition-bearing payloads opaquely, with explicit unsupported-pCID failure and no speculative parsing. That reduces accidental semantic overreach, but the specimen leaves condition-proof format and promise-accounting semantics to higher-layer pCID-defined protocols.
strengths: Explicit unknown-pCID policy allows safe store-and-forward of opaque payloads without speculative parsing.
The positional [pcid,payload] envelope gives a very clear layer boundary and preserves exact bytes for later audit.
Wrapper-based signatures/evidence can add integrity or authorship without forcing every lower layer to understand condition semantics.
The specimen does not require a central registry to make opaque carriage work.
weaknesses: The specimen does not define the condition object or proof model needed to verify conditional-release or geofencing semantics.
Auditability depends on external pCID handlers and wrapper protocols once payload semantics matter.
It does not spell out the promise/accounting rule that separates safe opaque carriage from authorized release behavior.
risks: A node could mistakenly treat successful opaque carriage as authorization to release or satisfy a condition.
Long-term preservation may keep bytes intact while losing the handler knowledge needed to interpret the condition reference.
Wrapper-only signing can make provenance discovery less uniform across implementations.
open_questions: What condition-reference format lets higher layers verify the condition object while lower layers remain opaque carriers?
What local promise-accounting record distinguishes storage/relay of opaque envelopes from acceptance of the embedded release condition?
How is durable pCID-to-spec resolution preserved for 100-year audits if handlers and organizations change?
assessment.authority_boundary: Evidence only; does not settle PromiseGrid design.
